1:
Augustine turns the closing phrase over carefully, since it will bear two senses. It may mean that Christ loved his own up to his death; but because his love is not ended by death, Augustine prefers that he loved them unto death, his love for them being what led him to it, and so led them to himself, for Christ is the end of the law (Romans 10:4). Chrysostom goes straight to the consequence rather than the construction, setting beside it Paul’s charge to be imitators of him as he is of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1): Christ taught us virtue not by words alone but by actions, and the foot-washing is meekness made visible (Matthew 11:29).

Ellicott marks the change in the Gospel’s own language about timing. Jesus had repeatedly said his hour was not yet come (John 2:4; 7:6), and now knows with equal certainty that the hour is at hand that he should depart to the Father. On the objects of the love, Ellicott takes his own to be the believers he had made sons of God, and Barnes reads the final clause of constancy, that he continued the proofs of his love until he was taken away by death.

On where the scene belongs there is no agreement. Robertson and most place it at the Last Supper, on our Thursday evening, the night before the crucifixion. Gill and Lightfoot set it earlier, at Bethany. Henry grants that the chronology is debated and holds the substance plain regardless, which is the sensible verdict: nothing in the verse depends on which evening it was.

Calvin explains why John opens here rather than with the institution the other Evangelists record. The Evangelist passes by what they had told in order to explain that Christ testified, by this visible sign, that the love with which he embraced his own was firm and lasting, so that though they were deprived of his presence they might still be convinced that death itself would not quench this love. On that reading the verse is the key to the chapter and to the Passion, since the washing, the giving of his body and the going to the cross all proceed from a love that, knowing the hour of departure, loves to the uttermost; and the greatness of the love is measured by the lowliness it stoops to.
2:
The familiar rendering misleads, and the grammarians correct it together. Robertson reads the participle as a genitive absolute meaning during supper, and gives his reason from the narrative itself, that the fourth verse shows plainly the meal was still going on. Ellicott prefers it now becoming supper time, observing that the supper was not ended but that the company had already reclined (compare vv.12, 26). Barnes agrees that the familiar translation expresses too much, the original meaning while they were at supper, which is clear from the fact that we find them still eating afterwards; he notes the Arabic and Persic versions give that sense where the Latin Vulgate reads as the English does. Clarke goes further and proposes while supper was preparing, arguing that the meal was probably not then begun, since the washing of feet was usually practised by the Jews before they entered on their meals (Luke 7:44); he also prefers the present participle on manuscript grounds, a reading he notes Origen had. Lightfoot acknowledges the aorist and still does not believe the supper was ended, comparing the same construction in the parallel account at Bethany. The scene is therefore set at a meal in progress or about to begin, not after one.

On the betrayal, Barnes glosses the idiom as the devil having cast it into the heart of Judas, comparing Paul’s fiery darts of the wicked (Ephesians 6:16) and the parallel notices elsewhere (Luke 22:3; Acts 5:3), and takes the sense to be that Satan inclined the mind of Judas to the act. Ellicott notes the better reading makes the clause say that the devil had put it into the heart that Judas should betray him, and rejects the alternative construal which would make it the devil’s own heart. Wesley reads the adverb as marking a first occasion, that the suggestion was probably now made for the first time. Robertson attends to John’s adverb, already, and finds it pertinent on two counts: Luke places Satan’s entering at the moment Judas offered to betray, and Jesus had seen a year before that Judas was a devil (John 6:70). The plot, in other words, is not news to anyone in the room except the eleven.

Calvin asks why the Evangelist mentions the betrayal at this exact point, and gives two answers. The first concerns Christ’s bearing: the notice shows the wonderful patience of Christ, who could endure to wash the feet of such a wicked and detestable traitor. The second concerns his timing, since Christ purposely selected the moment when he was near death for performing the last act of his life.

What John sets side by side, then, is a Lord about to humble himself in love and a disciple in whom the devil has already lodged the plot. The juxtaposition is deliberate and it governs how the next verses read: the love that loves to the end will kneel before Judas as before the rest, knowing exactly what is in his heart.
3:
Ellicott states the paradox the verse is built on, that it is with the full consciousness of his supreme power and divine origin that Jesus stoops to a slave’s task. Barnes puts the same measurement the other way round, that the dignity of his nature shows how low he would stoop to teach and save his people. Robertson notes the participle for knowing, repeated from the first verse, which accents the full consciousness of Jesus, and lists the three things known: that all things were given into his hands (compare Matthew 28:18; Matthew 11:27), that he came from God, and that he was going to God (John 16:28).

Ellicott then sets the clause expressly against the great passage on the self-emptying. Because Christ was conscious of all this, he left the disciples an example of the self-denial which is the necessary outcome of love; and the model is the one who, subsisting in the form of God, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). The knowledge is not incidental to the humility but its ground.

Clarke supplies the pastoral occasion. Knowing himself almost at the end of his race, Christ thought it necessary to leave the disciples a lesson of humility exemplified by himself, in order to deliver them from the bad influence of those false ideas of a worldly kingdom which their ambition had so often betrayed. The lesson is aimed at a specific fault in specific men, not offered in the abstract.

Calvin and the rest find in this the logic of the whole gospel, that it is not in ignorance of his greatness but in full knowledge of it that Christ humbles himself. The clause is therefore the hinge of the scene: the one into whose hands all things have been given, who came from God and returns to God, girds himself with a towel, so that the depth of the condescension is measured by the height it descends from. It is precisely the man who knows himself Lord of all who is free to take the lowest place, which is why the verse rebukes the disciples’ quarrel over precedence before a word is said about it.
4:
Clarke corrects a small misreading in the first clause, that he rose not from eating but from his place at table, the dishes probably not yet laid down though the guests were seated. Robertson marks the tense, a vivid dramatic present, and describes what was removed: the outer robe, leaving him in only the tunic, as one that serveth (Luke 22:27). Calvin makes the same point about the garment, that he laid aside the outer and not the inner, the people of Eastern countries wearing long robes. Wesley reduces it to the practical reason, that he laid aside the part of his clothing which would have hindered him. Barnes adds that it was customary to lay the mantle aside when working or running or in the heat of summer, and that girding oneself with a towel was the manner of a servant or slave (Luke 17:8).

Gill fills in what else was happening at that table, and the contrast is his point. Christ’s mind being intent on something else, and it being his meat and drink to do his Father’s will, he rises and leaves the disciples sitting to finish their meal; and he rises to wash their feet. Gill’s exclamation is the whole of his comment: amazing patience and humility.

Ellicott supplies the occasion from Luke, where there had been a strife among them which of them should be accounted the greatest. Luke places that dispute after the supper, but the words I am among you as he that serveth point almost certainly to a connection with this parabolic act. Ellicott infers that there had been some self-assertion in acts or omissions which Christ here rebukes, each of them perhaps claiming the place of honour above his brother. Robertson agrees that Jesus had already rebuked the apostles for their strife over precedence at the beginning of the meal (Luke 22:24–30).

The deliberateness is what the verse records. John tells the rising, the disrobing and the girding one motion at a time, and the reason for that fulness is that the man performing them is the Master. Every gesture belongs to a slave, and the Evangelist sets them down in order so that the question the act will raise cannot be evaded: if the Lord does this, what then are his servants to do?
5:
Gill notes that pouring the water was itself a servile work, properly belonging to servants, and he can even specify the vessel, since the rabbis had fixed the capacity of the basin used for washing feet at between two logs and nine kabs; a kab held about a quart and a log was a quarter of a kab. Lightfoot supplies the ruling behind that, from the day they made Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah president of the council, when the votes were numbered and they determined that the basin for washing feet should hold from two logs to ten. Ellicott and Robertson both note the definite article, that it was the basin in the room, commonly used and already standing ready, with the water at hand; and Ellicott draws the inference that matters, that everything was in place for one of the disciples to have performed this act which the Lord now performs.

Barnes explains the custom and the posture. It was uniformly the office of a servant to wash the feet of guests (1 Samuel 25:41), a matter of necessity where men travelled without shoes and reclined at meals; and the disciples were not sitting as we do but lying with their feet extended from the table, so that Jesus had easy access to them. Clarke cites the same precedent, Abigail answering David’s message by asking that her handmaid might be a servant to wash the feet of the servants of her lord. Lightfoot adds the general rule from the rabbis, that it was an unusual thing for superiors to wash the feet of inferiors, the duty running the other way.

Clarke records an old suggestion about the order, that some of the ancients supposed our Lord began with the feet of Judas, to inspire him with compunction and remorse, to melt him down with kindness, and to show all the disciples how they should act. Calvin reads the verse as stating a design rather than narrating the sequence, since the Evangelist adds that he began with Peter.

Two levels of meaning run through the act. Literally it is the lesson in humility that Christ will press home a few verses later, that if he washes their feet they ought to wash one another’s. Figuratively it opens the question of cleansing which he takes up himself at the tenth verse, the daily washing of feet soiled by the world’s dust that a man still needs after the bath. Calvin ties both back to the love named at the opening, since this is love that does not merely speak but kneels, taking the basin and the towel.
6:
Robertson catches the word order in Peter’s question, where the pronouns stand emphatically: dost thou my feet wash. He adds a plausible stage direction, that Peter may be supposed to have drawn his feet up as he spoke, in his impulsive humility. On whether Peter was the first to be washed, Ellicott calls it a point of no importance, while allowing that the natural impression of the narrative is that Peter’s turn came after that of at least one other.

The older interpreters read the order as significant. Origen pictures Christ as a physician who begins with those who want his attention most, washing the most unclean first and coming last to Peter, who needed the washing less than any. Theophylact and Chrysostom suggest instead that he washed the traitor first and came next to Peter, and they account for the silence of the rest by saying they were checked by the reply given to Peter, their silence being a sign not of want of love but of reverence.

Augustine enters into the feeling behind the protest and does not treat it as mere impulse. Who would not be filled with fear, he asks, at having his feet washed by the Son of God? He grants that it was a piece of the greatest audacity for the servant to contradict his Lord, and yet Peter preferred doing that to suffering his feet to be washed by his Lord and God.

Calvin weighs the same words more severely. The question expresses strong dislike of the action as foolish and unsuitable; and though the modesty in it would be worthy of commendation, it forgets what Calvin takes to be decisive, that obedience is of greater value in the sight of God than any kind of honour or service. Between them, Augustine and Calvin name both halves of what Peter is doing. The reverence is real, springing from a true sense of the gulf between the Lord and himself; and because it refuses what Christ commands, it becomes a humility that is its own kind of pride, which the next verses correct directly.
7:
Ellicott notices that the pronouns are picked up from Peter’s protest and turned back on him, so that the answer is a gentle rebuke: Peter’s words had almost implied that the Lord knew not what he was doing, when the opposite was really the case. Barnes and Ellicott agree about the reference of the promised knowing, taking it chiefly of the explanation Christ gives within a few minutes (vv.14–17), the symbolical act being made unforgettable by being first performed and then expounded. Robertson glosses the verb as knowing by experience, even if slowly. Clarke renders the sense as a request rather than a reproof: permit me to do it now, and I will shortly explain.

Calvin draws out the principle he finds enshrined in the sentence, that we ought simply to obey Christ even though we should not perceive the reason why he wishes this or that thing to be done. His analogy is domestic: as in a well-regulated house the head has the sole right to say what ought to be done, so that man is too haughty who refuses to obey the command of God because he does not know the reason of it.

Wesley applies the same thought to the believer’s whole walk rather than to this moment only. We do not now know perfectly any of his works, and it is enough that we can love and obey now, and that we shall know hereafter.

What the verse asks of Peter is therefore an order of priority, not a suspension of thought. He is not told that the act has no meaning, but that the meaning will come after the submission and not before it; and Christ keeps the promise within the quarter-hour. The posture it requires is the one Wesley describes for the rest of the Christian life, since much of what God does with his people is dark at the time and only afterwards seen to have had a purpose. To insist on understanding before submitting is to reverse the order, and Peter’s impatience to understand has to give way to the humility that obeys.
8:
Robertson marks the force of the refusal, a strong double negative amounting to never, and quotes Westcott’s judgment on what is at stake, that the first condition of discipleship is self-surrender; Peter’s act amounted to irreverence and want of confidence. Ellicott hears in the vehemence the very voice of the loving, impulsive but self-confident Peter of the earlier Gospels. Barnes draws the rule out of it, that we should yield to all the plain and positive requirements of God even if we cannot now see how obedience would promote his glory.

Gill traces the change in Peter’s bearing, that before he had behaved with modesty and now with obstinacy and perverseness; and though the words might arise from great reverence to Christ, they were wrong and rashly spoken, since Peter ought to have been satisfied with the reply already given and submitted, not knowing the reason then but assured he would know it afterwards. Clarke enters one limit on the severity of the threat, holding it certain that Christ did not mean to exclude him from the apostolic office should he persist in refusing out of the deepest reverence. Clarke and Wesley find the deeper sense in the answer, since the washing is emblematical of something spiritual. Wesley states it directly: if Christ does not wash a man in his blood and purify him by his Spirit, he can have no communion with him, nor any share in the blessings of his kingdom. The exchange has moved in one sentence from a question of courtesy to a question of belonging.

Calvin is sharp with Peter here, and distinguishes this refusal from the first. Hitherto Peter’s modesty was excusable; now he errs more grievously, because he has been corrected and still does not yield. Calvin names the fault in general terms, that it is a common thing for ignorance to be closely followed by obstinacy. Nor will the plea of reverence serve as a defence, since the very desire of showing respect for Christ is at fault where it does not absolutely obey the injunction.

The principle the verse turns on is therefore a hard one: to refuse the cleansing Christ offers, even out of reverence wrongly directed, is to refuse him altogether. The same self-will that will not be served by Christ cannot be saved by him, and only those who let him do for them what they cannot do for themselves have part with him. Peter’s threatened loss of everything is the warning to anyone who would dictate to his Lord the terms of his own cleansing.
9:
The same impulsive temper now runs the other way. Gill explains the reasoning behind the swing, that Peter, convinced everything depended on this washing and fearing to be deprived of communion with Christ, wishes to be cleansed entirely; Ellicott puts it as asking not for the feet only but for the whole man. Robertson quotes Dods’ summary of the reversal, that a moment ago Peter told his Master he was doing too much and now tells him he is doing too little. Barnes reads the ardour as a half-grasp of the spiritual meaning, since Peter now sees that his whole salvation and the entire question of his attachment to his Master are involved, and so asks for hands and head as well.

Calvin credits the yielding before faulting the excess. When Peter heard that he was ruined if he did not accept the cleansing, that necessity proved a sufficient instructor to tame him, and he lays aside opposition and yields. The yielding is real and Calvin says so plainly.

The error Calvin then identifies is a theological one rather than a failure of nerve. Peter goes wrong through thoughtlessness, treating as a thing of no value the benefit he had already received, as though he were altogether covered with pollution and needed a wholly new cleansing. What he has forgotten, in other words, is what has already been done for him. Wesley puts the whole of it more tenderly, that one would think man would be wiser than God, and yet this was well meant, being an ignorant earnestness.

The portrait is of a believer who, having been corrected, overcorrects: from refusing Christ’s grace to demanding more of it than is needed, and betraying in both that he has not understood. His extravagance is lovable in its way, since he would rather have too much of Christ than too little; but zeal without knowledge still misreads the Master’s mind, and the mistake is what opens the way for the next verse, where Christ measures out exactly how much washing a cleansed disciple requires. Ellicott states the premise Christ has to correct, that Peter’s words implied he was wholly unclean and needed a moral cleansing for feet and head and hands, for the whole man; and the answer will be that this was not so.
10:
Robertson and Ellicott both point out that everything turns on two different verbs. The man described as washed has bathed the whole body, and needs only to wash his feet, which is a different word for a partial cleansing. The picture is of someone coming from the bath to the table who has contracted dust on his feet along the way: he does not need another full washing but only the cleansing of what the walk has soiled.

Clarke supplies the practical background, taking the bathing literally, as something all the apostles had probably done recently in order to prepare themselves for the paschal solemnity, it being the custom of the Jews to bathe twice on that occasion; the feet then needed cleansing only of the dirt or dust that had adhered on the way. Gill reads the bath as regeneration and justification, the man washed in the blood of Christ being clean every whit and justified from all things, and he is careful to say that this is not by baptism but by Christ; the feet are the daily defilements of life, which need continual cleansing. Barnes calls the passage a difficult one and still arrives at the same distinction, between the man already cleansed and the daily renewal he requires. Calvin adds the qualification that keeps the word clean from being overstated, that believers are not called pure as though no stain at all remained in them, but because they are cleansed in their chief part, sin being deprived of its kingly power so that the righteousness of God holds the superiority; as one might call a body healthy that is not free of every ailment. Wesley puts the practical upshot in half a line, that having been already cleansed they need only to wash their feet, which is to walk holy and undefiled.

Augustine fastens instead on the exception at the end of the sentence, and notes that the Evangelist himself supplies the explanation in the verse following, that Christ knew who should betray him. The qualification is therefore not vague but pointed at one man in the room.

The doctrine the verse has long carried has two sides, and both are guards. Justification and regeneration are not repeated, so that a soul once washed by Christ is wholly clean before God and does not come back each day to be born again; and yet the believer walking through a defiling world contracts the dust of sin daily, and must come continually for the cleansing of confession and renewed grace. The first half meets the despair that fears it must be saved afresh after every fall, the second the presumption that once cleansed it needs no washing at all. And the closing clause adds a third guard, that no nearness to Christ and no outward rite cleanses a heart that harbours betrayal.
11:
The Evangelist is explaining his own earlier clause, and the explanation names a man without naming him. Barnes observes the exact distinction: Judas, though his feet were washed, was not clean in heart, the outward washing reaching the body but not the soul. Gill presses it further back, reading the want as a want of regeneration, since Judas was never truly washed in the deeper sense, never born again nor cleansed in the blood of Christ, so that his place among the disciples and his share in the foot-washing left him as defiled within as ever. The uncleanness is not a stain contracted at the table but a condition he brought to it, the betrayal having already been lodged in his heart (v.2).

Gill pushes the knowledge back as far as it will go, that Christ knew this not only from the beginning of his ministry when he chose the twelve, but from the beginning of time, this being fixed by the determinate counsel of God, to which he as the omniscient God was privy. Robertson observes what that knowledge did not alter, that Jesus had known for a year at least and yet treated Judas with his usual courtesy, and he asks whether Judas winced at the thrust. Ellicott and Robertson note what the aside tells us about the writer’s vantage point, since John, composing long afterwards, draws back the veil to show that Christ knew the traitor from the first. The reader is given information the eleven did not have, and given it before the betrayal is disclosed in the room.

Ellicott hears the clause as a warning rather than a verdict, spoken in the love which even then might have redeemed and cleansed the heart if it had been open to receive it. The lesson the verse presses is a hard one about proximity. The nearest place to Christ, at his table, under his hands, among his chosen, cannot of itself cleanse the heart. Judas received the same outward grace as Peter and John and remained unclean, because the inner washing of the Spirit was never his.

What the verse leaves is therefore a picture rather than an argument, and the picture is deliberately uncomfortable. Christ kneels before this man, takes his feet into his hands and washes them as carefully as the rest, knowing that the heart above them is already sold. The outward act of love is not withheld from the betrayer; neither does it cleanse him. The same basin, the same towel and the same Lord serve a man whose feet come away clean and whose soul does not.
12:
Christ now turns from the act to its exposition, keeping the promise he had made to Peter a few minutes earlier (v.7). Robertson notes the verb for taking his place again, that he reclined, and calls the question that follows a searching one, particularly as it reaches Simon Peter and Judas. Clarke and Origen observe that the Greek may be read as an imperative as well as a question, so that it would run consider what I have done, which would serve to rouse their minds and direct them to the meaning. Ellicott agrees about the function either way, that the question is asked not to be answered but to direct their attention to the interpretation which follows. Gill marks the completeness of the service in the opening clause, that the washing was performed to each of the twelve, Judas included.

Clarke weighs the grammatical question and comes down for the imperative, thinking it more likely that Christ gives a command here than asks a question, since he knew himself that they did not comprehend his design. Ellicott fixes the posture from the parallels, the reclining position customary at meals, and notes what it implies about the order of events, that the washing preceded the supper. Augustine sees Christ mindful of his promise to Peter and now beginning to teach him, so that the question is the first instalment of the explanation owed. Alcuin finds a mystery in the resuming of the garments, reading it as an image of the risen Lord taking up his glory again after the humiliation.

Calvin explains why an explanation is needed at all, since what Christ had said about the spiritual washing was a sort of digression from his main design, and had it not been for Peter’s opposition he would not have spoken on that subject. Now he returns to what he meant from the first. Calvin states the purpose of the whole transaction without ornament. Christ discloses the reason of what he had done, namely that he wishes to be followed by all the godly, so that none might grudge to descend to a service for his brethren and equals, however mean and low that service might be.

The method is as deliberate as the lesson. Christ does not merely command humility; he performs it first and explains it afterwards, so that the teaching is fixed in the memory by sight before it is pressed home in words. The question invites the disciples to interpret the act for themselves, and prepares them for the rule he is about to lay down, that what the Lord has done to them they must do to one another.
13:
Ellicott distinguishes the two titles, taking the first for Teacher rather than the Hebrew Rabbi in this place, and Barnes takes the second of the reverence due to a sovereign and ruler (compare Matthew 23:8–10). Gill and Lightfoot note that Rabbi and Mar were the honoured titles Jewish pupils gave their doctors, and that the disciples gave them to Christ not out of flattery but reverence; Clarke recalls the double title reserved for the most accredited teachers. Robertson marks the emphatic pronoun and the verb for calling, which means to address with a title, and compares the titular form here with Thomas’s confession, my Lord and my God (John 20:28). Lightfoot adds that the two titles were in frequent use among the doctors of Jerusalem and of Babylon alike, and Ellicott cites the rule from the Sanhedrin tractate that no pupil was permitted to call his teacher by his proper name. Barnes notes how far the second title travelled, being given to Christ many hundred times in the New Testament.

What the expositors fasten on is the frankness of the acceptance. Christ does not disclaim the dignity but confirms it, and Barnes states what is being confirmed: that he was their Teacher and Instructor and also their Sovereign and King. The sentence is a premise rather than a digression.

The argument of the next verse depends on it entirely. Had Christ been a fellow-servant performing a courtesy, the washing would prove nothing about what the disciples owe each other; because he is in fact what they call him, his stooping binds them. The higher the rank conceded, the heavier the obligation that follows from the act.

There is also a false humility the acceptance rules out. Christ does not pretend to be less than he is in order to serve; being truly Lord and Master, he serves, and that is the glory of the condescension rather than an awkwardness in it. The pattern set for his people is accordingly not to disown their station but, whatever it is, to spend it in love for others. The greatness is real and the stooping is real, and the lesson lies in the two held together rather than in either alone.
14:
Calvin identifies the form of the argument as one from the greater to the less, and Ellicott spells out the inference: if the Lord himself stoops so low, much more must the disciples humble themselves for one another. Robertson notes the first-class condition, which concedes the fact rather than supposing it, and glosses the verb rendered ought as owing a debt, so that the obligation rests on them to render this or any other needed service.

Whether a literal rite is enjoined is the question the verse has always raised, and Barnes argues at length that it is not. The foot-washing was a rite of hospitality among the Jews, a common and well-known thing performed by servants, and it is the manifest design of the command to teach humble service rather than to institute a ceremony alongside baptism and the Supper. Wesley presses the same case with an argument from silence that is hard to answer: why do we never read of any one apostle washing the feet of another? Because they understood their Lord better, and he never designed the words to be literally taken, but to teach the great lesson of humble love.

Calvin names the obstacle the command is aimed at, which is not ignorance but pride. Pride hinders us from maintaining the equality that ought to exist among us; and Christ, far exalted above all others, stoops down in order to make ashamed the proud men who think themselves not bound to hold intercourse with the brethren.

What is required, then, is a disposition rather than a ceremony: the readiness to perform for one another even the meanest offices of love. The literal act is the parable, and the thing commanded is the lowly, mutual service it pictures. If the Lord and Master has washed the feet of his servants, no follower of his may count any service too low or any brother beneath his help, and the towel passes from Christ’s hands into theirs. Clarke spells out what that means in practice: they should be ready, after his example, to condescend to all the weakness of their brethren, to be willing to do the meanest offices for them, and to prefer the least of them in honour to themselves. Ellicott notices a small deliberate touch in the wording, that the two titles are repeated from the previous verse but in the inverse order, which throws the emphasis where the argument needs it. Calvin presses the question the proud man never asks himself: what does a mortal man imagine himself to be, when he refuses to bear with his brethren? Wesley adds that the washing was meant to do two things at once, to teach the great lesson of humble love and also to confer inward purity upon them.
15:
Ellicott locates the example in the principle and not in the specific act, and rests the distinction on the grammar: the clause does not say that which I have done to you but according as I have done to you, so that the imitation is to be worked out by applying the same principle of love and self-sacrifice in all the varying circumstances of life. Robertson glosses the noun as an illustration set before the eyes, and notes that Peter, with this incident evidently in mind, calls Christ a pattern (1 Peter 5:3; compare 1 Peter 2:21).

Gill marks out which of Christ’s acts are imitable and which are not. He is an example to his people in the exercise of grace, of meekness, humility, love and patience, and in the discharge of duty, in submission to ordinances and in attending on them, and in the several duties owed both to those without and to those within; but not in his miracles or his mediatorial work, which no one can copy. The distinction is not a hedge but a necessity, since the alternative is a discipleship that attempts the impossible and neglects the commanded.

Calvin guards the same point and then gives it an edge, holding that we are not at liberty to take all Christ’s actions without reserve as subjects of imitation. He turns it against those who keep the forty days’ fast of Lent on the strength of Christ’s example, observing that Christ never intended to lay down his fast as a rule for others.

The result is a discriminating discipleship that keeps both the force and the freedom of the example. We are bound to copy the humility and the love absolutely; we are not bound to reproduce the basin and the towel. So the command neither shrinks into a ceremony nor evaporates into a sentiment, but lays on every disciple the duty of rendering, in his own time and place, the same self-forgetting service his Lord rendered at the supper. Robertson notes that the word for example is common in the papyri for an illustration or a warning and appears elsewhere in the New Testament in James, Second Peter and Hebrews, so that what Christ sets before the disciples is of a recognised kind: a thing done once in order to be read off and applied.
16:
The saying is proverbial and Christ uses it more than once, in this Gospel and in Matthew (Matthew 10:24; John 15:20). Robertson sets out the two comparisons it draws, slave against lord and the one sent against the one who sent him. Clarke would render the second term as apostle, and takes the whole saying as aimed at the suppression of all worldly ambition and lordly conduct in the apostles and their successors in the ministry. Barnes draws a different consequence from the same words, that the disciples were to manifest the same spirit their Master did and to expect the same treatment from the world (Matthew 10:25).

Gill marks the weight of the opening formula, the doubled asseveration being used when something of moment and importance, worthy of attention, is about to be delivered. Robertson states the substance of it plainly, that Jesus here enforces the dignity of service, and notes that he argues the same point at a little more length in Luke (Luke 22:27). Augustine sums the scene in a phrase, that Christ said this because he had washed the disciples’ feet, as the Master of humility both by word and by example. The proverb is not a new argument but the compression of the one the act had already made.

The logic runs opposite to the world’s. Where men reason that the greater need not serve the less, Christ reasons that since the greatest has served, none of the lesser may refuse; and the conclusion is inescapable on the premise the disciples have just conceded. A servant who claims exemption from lowly service is claiming to be greater than his lord, which is the absurdity the foot-washing has just exposed in action.

The saying cuts hardest at pride of office. If even the apostles, the sent ones, are not above their Sender, then no minister or office-bearer in the church may lord it over the flock or count any service beneath his rank. Clarke’s application is the natural one: the verse stands as a perpetual rebuke to ambition among Christ’s ministers, recalling them to the towel rather than the throne. Clarke draws the positive side of the same thought, that Christ has ennobled the acts of humility by practising them himself, so that the true glory of a Christian consists in being, in his measure, as humble as his Lord. Calvin enters one caution about how far to press the saying: these are proverbial sayings which admit of a far more extensive application, and they ought to be accommodated to the case in hand, so that those are mistaken who take them generally, as though Christ were here exhorting his disciples to bear the cross. Wesley applies it to both halves of discipleship, that a servant not greater than his lord ought therefore to think much neither of doing nor of suffering the same things.
17:
The sentence is built of two conditions, knowing and doing, and Robertson marks both. Ellicott locates the blessing precisely: it lies in the doing and not in the knowing. Barnes and Gill draw the practical consequence, that to understand Christ’s teaching about humility and not practise it is to forfeit the happiness the teaching promises, since the beatitude is reserved for those who carry the lesson into life.

Clarke states where happiness actually lies, that it consists in the knowledge of God and in obedience to him, and that a man is not happy because he knows much but because he receives much of the divine nature and is in all his conduct conformed to the divine will. Ellicott notes that the first clause assumes their knowledge, these being old lessons taught before in word and now taught in act and word together, and that their knowledge had not profited them hitherto. What the words warn against is a particular self-deception, the supposing that to grasp a duty is to have discharged it. It is possible to know these things clearly and even to admire them while remaining proud and unserving; and knowledge of that kind does not bless but increases responsibility.

Calvin presses the same distinction into a definition, holding that knowledge is not entitled to be called true unless it produces such an effect on believers as to lead them to conform themselves to their Head; on the contrary it is a vain imagination when we look upon Christ, and the things belonging to Christ, as separate from ourselves. Robertson notes that both clauses are conditions, the second assuming a continued practice rather than an occasional act, since just knowing does not bring happiness and neither does just occasional doing. Augustine states the pronouncement in its plainest form, that blessed they shall be if they do them. The happiness is pronounced not on the learned but on the obedient, which is why the clause is cast as a condition rather than a promise.

The verse therefore closes the foot-washing on its sharpest edge. Christ has performed the act, accepted his titles, drawn the lesson and sealed it with a proverb, and now lays the whole of it on the conscience. To know the way of humble love is good and to walk in it is blessed; and the clearness with which the duty has been set before these men is exactly what leaves them without excuse if they fail to practise it. So the scene stops being something to admire and becomes something to obey, with the blessing attached only to those who, having seen and understood, go and do the same.
18:
The exception is entered against the beatitude just pronounced, and it is entered deliberately. When Christ has called the disciples clean and happy, he excludes one of them from both. Barnes takes the clause about choosing of the choice to apostleship (compare John 6:70; Luke 6:13), since Judas was chosen to the office though never cleansed in heart; the two senses of choosing have to be kept apart or the verse will seem to charge God with the betrayal. Ellicott notes the emphatic I know, and the consequence that nothing in what follows takes Christ by surprise.

The Scripture quoted is from the Psalter, where the man who ate bread with the sufferer lifted up his heel against him (Psalm 41:9), the image being of a table-companion turning to kick like a vicious beast. The force of the citation lies in the relationship it names rather than in the violence: one bound by the sacred ties of shared food and trust, which is what makes the act the basest kind of treachery. That Christ should apply these words at this supper, having a few minutes earlier washed the man’s feet, is what the expositors find most striking in the verse.

Chrysostom dwells on the fall itself rather than the prophecy, observing that it is a grievous thing to come to the depths of wickedness, for then the soul becomes hard to be restored; and he marvels that Judas, enjoying great assistance, fell nonetheless.

Calvin explains why the warning is spoken aloud at all, and finds two purposes in it. Christ declares that there is one among the disciples who is the very reverse of a disciple, partly for the sake of Judas, in order to render him the more inexcusable, and partly for the sake of the others, that they may not be overpowered by the ruin of Judas. The betrayal is therefore set before the eleven in advance as a thing written long before, so that when treachery appears at the Lord’s own table it will not shake them. The betrayal is thus presented as neither an accident nor a defeat, but as a thing foreseen, written long before, and disclosed in advance by the one person in the room who already knew it.
19:
Robertson renders the opening adverb as from now on, and parses the three clauses in order: before it comes to pass, whenever it does come to pass, and the purpose, that they may keep on believing. He notes that the claim being confirmed is the one Christ has made repeatedly in this Gospel (John 8:24), and that the same purpose is stated again later (John 14:29). Gill reduces the clause to its plain content, that Christ gave them notice beforehand that one of them should betray him.

Barnes explains the evidential force the fulfilment would have. By it they would see that he had a knowledge of the heart and the power of foretelling future events, and must therefore have been sent by God; and Barnes is careful that this does not imply they had no faith before, only that their faith would be increased and strengthened. Clarke agrees that the frequent predictions of his death, so circumstantial as they were, tended to confirm the disciples not only in the belief that he was the Messiah but in the belief of his omniscience.

Ellicott adds the consideration that makes the forewarning necessary rather than merely helpful. Had Christ not declared his knowledge of all this, and traced even his choice of Judas to the will of God, there would have been room for doubt whether that choice was consistent with his being the Messiah. The prediction forestalls an objection the betrayal would otherwise have raised.

Calvin generalises the comfort beyond this one event. The statement reminds the disciples that when one of their number becomes a reprobate, this is so far from being a good reason for discouragement that it ought to be a fuller confirmation of their faith. His reasoning runs through the whole of Scripture: if we did not see before our eyes, in the Church, what has been foretold about her distresses and struggles, a doubt might justly arise asking where the prophecies are; but when the truth of Scripture agrees with our daily experience, we perceive more clearly that God takes care of us and that we are governed by his providence. Calvin adds the qualification that keeps the verse honest, that the treachery of Judas was not the first thing that led the disciples to faith, but the thing by which their faith made greater progress.
20:
The saying appears also in the earlier Gospels (Matthew 10:40), and its placing here is what the expositors try to account for. Ellicott traces the connection to the disciples’ commission: having spoken of their being sent as his servants, of the betrayal by one of their number, and of his foretelling it, Christ now bids them go forth and be content if their path is the one their Master has trodden, not disheartened by treachery even in their own midst.

Chrysostom marvels at the dignity being conferred and puts it as a question, asking what can be equal to the receiving of Christ and his Father. The chain runs in both directions: to welcome the apostle is to welcome the one who sent him, and through him the Father. Clarke reads the same words as encouragement about the mission’s prospects, that though the disciples should be rejected by many they would be received by several, and whoever received them should reap the utmost benefit. Wesley compresses the whole into one clause, that Christ puts his own honour upon them as his ambassadors.

Chrysostom finds a close and harmonious connection where others find none, and explains the mechanism: when the apostles were about to go forth and suffer many dreadful things, Christ comforted them in two ways, one derived from himself and one derived from others. Barnes is franker about the difficulty, saying that why Christ repeats the saying at this time cannot now be known, and that it is not closely connected with the subject of the conversation; but he offers a conjecture worth weighing, that it was to show how intimately united Christ, his Father, his apostles and all who receive them are. On that reading the verse has a dark corollary: the man who betrays Christ betrays, for the same reason, God, so that Judas was about to betray not a person only but the cause of religion in the world. Calvin judges that Christ intended by this to provide against a particular scandal, the stumbling that Judas’s crime might cause among the rest. His reason for thinking the precaution needed is drawn from experience rather than from the text, since there is too good evidence that we are very ready to be wounded by the falls of those who hold office. Against that he sets the assurance Christ gives, that their ministry stands in unbroken union with himself and with the Father, whatever one apostate may do.

The placing is therefore deliberate and tender. In the same breath in which he speaks of betrayal, Christ exalts the mission of the men who will remain, so that the sin of one shall not shake the confidence of the eleven. It is worth noticing which way the care runs: troubled in spirit himself, he turns to dignify and steady them. The apostate falls and the apostleship stands, carrying Christ and God to all who receive it.
21:
Augustine raises the obvious question about the trouble and dismisses the obvious answer. Did the betrayal occur then for the first time to his mind? It did not; he was now about to make the traitor known and single him out from the rest, and was troubled in spirit for that reason. Augustine insists on the location of the trouble, that it was not in flesh but in spirit, and that it was by his own will, as at the grave of Lazarus (John 11:33). Chrysostom supplies another occasion for it, that having twice promised help to the apostles in their future labours, Christ remembers that the traitor is cut off from both, and is troubled at the thought.

Augustine presses the question further and answers it from the context. Christ had a little before quoted the psalm about the man who ate bread with him lifting up his heel, and earlier still had said that they were not all clean, so that nothing here is new to him. Augustine then gives a second reason for the trouble beyond the unmasking: Christ was troubled at the thought of his Passion being so near at hand, and at the dangers to which his faithful followers would be brought at the hand of the traitor. He adds a purpose served by the trouble itself, that our Lord deigned to be troubled in order to show that false brethren cannot be cut off from the Church without grief. Barnes grounds the agitation in Christ’s true humanity, saying he was deeply affected with the ingratitude and wickedness of a professed friend, his tender sensibilities being affected not less deeply than those of other men would be by baseness and treason. Clarke attends to the verb for testifying, which means that he spoke with great earnestness, and raises the question whether even now Christ sought Judas’s benefit, that he might repent.

The doubled asseveration marks how far the disclosure has advanced. Earlier he had said only that they were not all clean (v.10); now he states plainly that one of them shall betray him. The hint has become an announcement, though still without a name. Wesley notes the advantage of that reticence, that speaking thus indefinitely at first was profitable to them all, since it set every man to examining himself rather than his neighbour.

What the trouble measures is the nature of the wound. The Lord who speaks of his own coming death without agitation is moved to the depths by the treachery of a man he had chosen, taught and a few minutes earlier served on his knees. And the announcement is itself a last appeal, since by declaring openly that one of them would do it, Christ names the sin before it is committed and leaves the door of repentance standing open. The plainness of the warning is what afterwards leaves the traitor without excuse.
22:
Gill describes the look as that of men surprised and astonished, scarcely crediting what was said, having had no suspicion of anyone among them capable of such an action; and he offers two readings of the glances, that they expressed detestation and indignation at so horrible an iniquity, or else that each was watching to see whether any man’s countenance would betray him. Barnes glosses the word for doubting as that kind of anxiety a man feels when he is in perplexity and knows not what to say or do, and renders it that they were at a loss.

Ellicott gathers what the other Gospels add. Matthew and Mark both state that the disciples put their doubt into words, and Luke’s narrative implies the questioning but has it addressed to one another rather than to Christ. What John remembers is the look of astonishment and the way each tried to read the countenance of his brother; and Ellicott notes why John would remember it, since he was nearest to our Lord and knew what the others may not have known, how Peter beckoned to him and how he put the question. Robertson observes that this is the moment Leonardo caught in the Last Supper, adding drily that the figures are painted like the monks for whom the work was made.

Calvin reads the distribution of unease as the point of the scene. Those who are conscious of no crime are rendered uneasy by what Christ has said, while Judas alone is so stupid amid his malice that he remains unmoved. The explanation he gives is about reverence: the authority of Christ stood so high with the disciples that they were convinced he said nothing without good reason, where Satan had expelled all reverence from the heart of Judas, so that it was harder than a rock.

Calvin then defends Christ against the charge of needless cruelty in the ambiguity. Though he appears somewhat unkind in inflicting this torture for a time on men who were innocent, the anxiety was profitable to them and so he did them no injury; it is proper that when the children of God have heard the sentence of the ungodly they should feel uneasiness, that they may sift themselves and guard against hypocrisy. The scene therefore both warns and commends: outward fellowship is no guarantee of inward truth, since a traitor sat undetected among the twelve, and yet the instinct to suspect oneself rather than a neighbour is the mark of a tender conscience.
23:
Gill, Lightfoot and Robertson explain the posture before the intimacy. At such a meal the guests lay on couches propped on the left arm, so that the man placed next to Jesus would naturally rest, when he turned, against his breast; Robertson marks the phrase as naming the place of nearest fellowship at the table. The unnamed disciple is John himself, who throughout this Gospel veils his name under the loving title, a reticence Augustine notes as the Evangelist’s own way of designating himself.

Lightfoot supplies the seating rules from the rabbis, that they ate leaning on the left side with their feet to the ground; that where there were two couches the chief person lay highest and the second above him, so that the second man’s place was by the first man’s bolster; and that if the chief wished to speak with his neighbour he had to raise himself and sit upright, since he could not talk while leaning. Barnes guards against a misunderstanding of the English, that John was not actually lying on Christ’s bosom at that moment but occupied the place next to him, so that his head would naturally fall back toward it when he spoke. Clarke and Wesley describe the same arrangement, and Wesley suggests that Christ may now have given John the first proof of his peculiar love by disclosing this secret to him. Bede reads the posture as a sign as well as a fact. John’s lying in the bosom and upon the breast was not only an evidence of present love but also a token of the future, of those new and mysterious doctrines which he was afterwards commissioned to reveal to the world. Augustine presses the figure through the word itself, asking what else is signified by bosom but secret, and calling it the hollow of the breast, the secret chamber of wisdom; so that the disciple who leaned there became the channel of the loftiest revelation.

The placing of the detail is what gives it force. While the rest of the table looks round in dismay, one disciple is resting against his Master, near enough both to be asked and to ask; and it is that nearness, not any office, which makes him the man through whom the secret will pass.

The fathers take the arrangement as an emblem of what is open to any believer. To lean on the breast of Christ is to be admitted to his closest confidence, near enough to hear the secrets of his heart; and on their reading John’s place at the table pictures the intimacy to which the gospel calls every disciple, from which flow both the knowledge of Christ’s mind and the freedom to ask him what one longs to know. The nearer the heart rests on him, the more freely it may inquire.
24:
Gill reconstructs the difficulty Peter was in. He perhaps lay at some distance from Christ, or in such a position that he could not whisper to him himself; and he knew besides that John might use more freedom, being admitted to greater familiarity. So he beckoned, which Gill says was a usual expedient at meals when the posture of the company made conversation impossible, the sign being made by pointing with the hands and fingers or by a nod of the head.

Ellicott notes that the Greek is present tense, so that Peter beckons or makes a sign, and he reads the appeal as resting on an assumption about John: Peter supposes that the disciple whom Jesus loved is more than any other in the confidence of his Master, and that he already knows who is meant, and signs to him to tell what he knows. Ellicott also explains why Peter turns to this man in particular, since the two had both been disciples of the Baptist (John 1:40–41) and were companions and friends in the later work as in the earlier (compare Acts 3:1).

Robertson glosses the verb as nodding and reads Peter’s character out of the gesture, that he was cautious but could not contain his curiosity; and he notes the practical advantage of John’s position, being in front of Jesus and so able to have a whispered word with him. The better text, Ellicott observes, makes Peter’s message an imperative rather than a report: say who it is of whom he speaketh.

The small arrangement is a vivid touch of eye-witness detail and also a study in two temperaments. Peter, ever forward, must know at once and yet defers to another man’s nearness; John, resting where he rests, is the one fitted to ask. It shows the company in their confusion turning instinctively to the disciple closest to the Master’s heart, each using the place he has, the bold prompting and the beloved asking, so that the answer may be drawn out for all of them. Chrysostom names the reason John held that place, and will not look for a subtler one: others were loved, but he was loved more than any, and the familiarity is simply love.
25:
The word for the posture here differs from the one used two verses earlier, and that change of word is made to carry the sense. Barnes explains that it means falling back, or laying his head back on the bosom of Jesus, so that he could speak to him privately without being heard by the others; Robertson marks the participle for falling back and adds that it was easily done from where he lay. Clarke infers the same from the secrecy of what follows, that John altered his position at table in order to ask, and that he asked by whispering, since the other disciples had not heard what he said, as the narrative shows a few verses later (v.28). Wesley puts it in a phrase, leaning down and so asking him privately.

Gill pictures the movement exactly: lying on the couch just in front of Jesus with his back toward him, John bends backwards, falls on his breast and whispers in his ear. Ellicott notes that several good authorities, including the Vatican and Cambridge manuscripts, add the word thus, describing the action as it took place, though the balance of authority is against the insertion; and he observes that the English preserves the change of words from the earlier verse without quite conveying it, since there the disciple reclines toward his Master’s bosom and here he leans back upon his breast. Clarke supposes the answer came the same way, the words about the morsel being whispered back by Christ to John. What the question keeps is as notable as what it seeks. John does not call out across the table or demand an answer aloud; he draws close and asks softly, and he still says Lord. The address keeps the reverence inside the closeness, and the whisper keeps the secret inside the asking.

The arrangement also explains why the answer could be given at all. A secret of this weight could not be cried out in the room without doing to Judas publicly what Christ had so far declined to do, and it is entrusted instead to the one disciple near enough to hear it and discreet enough to hold it.

So the verse shows the two things the company needed held together. The eleven are desperate to know and cannot ask; the man who can ask is the one resting against his breast. He asks the one thing they all long to know, in the posture of love and trust, and his private question draws a private answer, by which the traitor is shown to one man only until the deed itself discloses what the sign had quietly said.
26:
Robertson explains the morsel, a word found only here in the New Testament, and the custom behind it, since it was a token of intimacy to allow a guest to dip his bread in the common dish (compare Ruth 2:14; Mark 14:20). Lightfoot and Clarke note that for the host to dip and then hand the sop to a particular guest was a very unusual thing, which is why the others at the table are likely to have read it as a mark of favour, or as Christ sending Judas out on some errand, and so missed the meaning entirely. Wesley draws out the care in it, that Jesus answered John in his ear, so careful was he not to offend, if it had been possible, even Judas himself; and he adds that the other disciples probably thought Judas peculiarly happy.

Augustine meets the objection the next verse will raise, that Satan entered Judas after he had received bread from Christ’s hand, and asks whether this was the worth of Christ’s bread. His answer is that the morsel was not poison but a sign, the guilt lying in the heart that received a token of love while plotting murder.

Calvin asks why a sign was used at all, when Christ might simply have named the man. His answer turns on who was meant to know: the sign was of such a nature that it discovered Judas to one person only, so that John might be a witness of the fact and reveal it at the proper time, while Christ intentionally delayed the public exposure.

What the sop amounts to is therefore an act of restraint and an appeal at once. The Lord points out his betrayer not with an accusing word but with a gift, handing the morsel of friendship to the man about to sell him, and disclosing the secret only to the disciple who could keep it. That the appeal is refused makes what follows darker; that it was made at all is the measure of a love which, having washed this man’s feet, now feeds him from its own hand. The last thing Christ does for Judas is a kindness.
27:
Robertson notes that this is the only place in the Gospel where the name Satan occurs, and the sequence matters: the devil had before this put the plan into Judas’s heart (v.2; Luke 22:3), and now enters to confirm and hurry the deed. Ellicott fixes the instant precisely, that it was then, when the heart hardened itself to receive from Jesus the sacred pledge of love while it was plotting in black hatred how to betray him, that the possession became complete. Barnes supplies a motive from the circumstances, that Judas, seeing Jesus knew his plan and that the others would soon know it, was aroused by sudden anger and resolved to execute it at once.

Lightfoot reads a typology into the moment, that as Satan had entered into the serpent which deceived the first Adam, so the second Adam could not be betrayed but by one into whom he should first enter.

On the words Christ then speaks, the expositors are careful about their force. Wesley insists it is not a permission, much less a command, but as if he had said that if Judas is determined to do it, why does he delay; and the effect is to show him that he could not be hid, while expressing Christ’s own readiness to suffer. Clarke agrees, judging Judas past all counsel by this point, and reading the words as those of a master of his own hour who would not have the dark business drawn out. Clarke also rejects outright the notion that the sop was the Lord’s Supper, calling it an utter mistake.

The verse is therefore the point of no return, and it is grace refused rather than grace withheld that makes it so. Love’s last appeal, the morsel from Christ’s hand, only hardens the man who takes it, and Satan enters where grace is finally declined. The calm instruction to be quick about it is the word of one who is not being overtaken by events but setting the hour of his own betrayal, going to death as the Lord who lays down his life and not as the victim of Judas.
28:
The sign and the whispered answer had disclosed the traitor to one man only, so that the rest, hearing nothing but the instruction to be quick, did not connect it with the betrayal at all. Gill and Barnes note the ignorance as a simple fact of the scene. Ellicott reads the sentence as a comment of the Apostle’s own, written in remembrance of the impression made at the time: they heard the words spoken to Judas, but none of them knew until afterwards that those words referred to the betrayal. Robertson states it plainly, that the disciples had not yet perceived the treacherous heart of Judas.

Gill limits the ignorance precisely, that not one of those who lay upon the couches knew, excepting John, to whom the signal had been given. Barnes draws the same conclusion about the sign, that this shows Jesus had signified to John only who it was that should betray him; and he explains the disciples’ supposition about the bag, the travelling purse in which they put their common property, and about the feast, which continued seven days, so that they supposed Christ had directed Judas to provide for their wants during them. Calvin asks the harder question, why the knowledge John now possessed did not spread at once, and offers two answers. Either John had not yet related to the others what Christ had told him, or else they were so much struck by it that they lost their presence of mind; and Calvin thinks it probable that John himself was almost out of his senses.

From that he draws a lesson about the church rather than about the eleven. What then happened to the disciples we frequently see taking place in the Church, that few of the believers discern the hypocrites whom the Lord loudly condemns. The failure of discernment is not a peculiar weakness of that night but a standing condition.

The warning the verse leaves is therefore directed at anyone inclined to trust outward fellowship. The eleven sat at the same table as the traitor and could not tell him from themselves; he was hidden in the holiest company, at the moment of his own unmasking, because the sign meant for John meant nothing to them. The searching knowledge of hearts belongs to Christ alone, who saw in Judas what no disciple at that table discerned, and who had just said so in words the room could not interpret.
29:
The misreading had a natural basis in the man’s office. Gill and Barnes recall that Judas had the bag, the common purse of the company (compare John 12:6), so that when Christ told him to be quick the others supposed the treasurer was being sent on an ordinary errand: either to buy what was needed against the feast, or to give something to the poor, which was a customary act of charity at the Passover season. Ellicott and Robertson note how exactly the guess fits the office he held, and the irony follows from that fit, since the very trust that made him the thief made him the natural man to send on such business.

Robertson treats the supposition as mere inference in their ignorance, and notes what it implies about the timing: the feast of unleavened bread began after the passover meal and lasted eight days, so that if this evening stood twenty-four hours ahead of that meal there was no hurry at all, the next day being ample. Ellicott suggests what sort of gift they had in mind, since such gifts seem to have been made at all festivals, and their thought was probably of enabling the poor to obtain the lamb and the other requisites for keeping the Passover. Calvin draws a small but telling inference from the guess itself: it is plain from other passages how great Christ’s poverty was, and yet out of the little he had he gave to the poor, since the Apostles would never have conjectured that he had spoken about almsgiving if it had not been his usual custom. Clarke adds a chronological observation he takes from Calmet, and it bears on the harmony of the Gospels. Since the disciples supposed Judas was going out to buy for the feast, and on the day of the passover there was neither buying nor selling in Jerusalem, this supper cannot have been the Passover meal itself but the evening before.

What the verse mainly does, though, is measure the completeness of the deception. The eleven, suspecting nothing, imagine their fellow on an errand of provision or of mercy at the precise moment he is going out to sell their Master for thirty pieces of silver.

The bag is the detail that carries the irony. The purse that marked him as trusted steward, and that should have served the poor, becomes the cover of the deed; and the innocence of the disciples’ guesses is the exact measure of how thoroughly he had concealed himself. The traitor passes from the table of his Lord under the guise of a servant on holy business, with the good opinion of every man in the room.
30:
Robertson marks the haste in the adverb, that Judas went out immediately, the deed now set in motion and the supper left behind. The departure is the first thing the verse records and the shortest; everything else hangs on the three words that close it.

Lightfoot reckons what the errand involved, since the man had two miles to go from Bethany to Jerusalem, and then had to seek out the chief priests, get them together and make his bargain; whether he did all of it that same evening or the day following, Lightfoot thinks Scripture says nothing and the question is of no great moment. Wesley adds what became of him afterwards, that he went out to the chief priests and returned, being with them when they ate the passover though not at the Lord’s Supper. Robertson and Ellicott agree that the final clause is doing more than fixing the hour. On the surface it is a simple note of time, telling when Judas went; but the Evangelist surely intends a further sense, the symbolic darkness into which the traitor passed. He went out from the light of the world (John 8:12) into the night, both the night of the hour and the night of his own soul.

Ellicott is careful about how much may be claimed, saying we cannot assert that the writer meant the words to express more than the physical fact, and yet that we feel in them a fulness of meaning which cannot have been unintentional. Robertson notes that darkness falls suddenly in the orient, so that the remark is literally exact as well as ominous. Clarke puts the two senses together in one clause, that under the conduct of the prince of darkness, and in the time of darkness, Judas went to do this work of darkness. The contrast the sentence draws is between inside and outside. Within, the light still shone, the love still spoke and the Master still taught; without lay the darkness into which this man plunged, having refused the last morsel of grace offered him. It was night in every sense the words will carry: the night of the world’s darkest deed, the night of a lost soul, and the night before the cross.

The departure also clears the room. Once the traitor has gone out, Christ turns to the eleven who remain and opens to them the new commandment and the promises of the upper room, so that the going-out of the man who chose darkness becomes the threshold of the brightest teaching of the supper. What the three words leave behind them is a short account of apostasy: to turn from Christ is to go out into the night, and there is no darker night than that of a man who has sat at this table, been served by these hands, and gone out to sell the host.
31:
Everything turns on the adverb. Robertson reads it as now at last, the crisis having come, with a sense of deliverance from the presence of Judas and of surrender to the Father’s will; and he notes the aorist, which marks the consummation of glory in death for both the Son and the Father, the verb sounding four times in these two verses. Barnes explains what has just been completed: the last deed is done that was necessary to secure the death of the Son of man, and with it the glory resulting from that death, the success of the gospel and the exaltation of the Messiah. Clarke paraphrases the claim being made, that now it fully appears he is the person appointed to redeem a lost world by his blood, having been glorified already by the appointment and about to be glorified further by his death, resurrection and ascension.

Ellicott explains why the glory can be spoken of as present when the suffering is still to come. The going out of Judas is the sign that the betrayal and death were at hand; in that lay the glory of the accomplished work, and it lies so immediately before him that it is at once realised, the brightness of the vision overpowering all thought of the darkness of the path which leads to it. Origen dates the moment the same way, that after the glory of the miracles and the transfiguration, the next glorifying of the Son of man began when Judas went out, and he reads the death as the triumph in which Christ spoiled principalities and powers and made a show of them openly (Colossians 2:15).

Calvin explains the pastoral need the saying met. The last hour was at hand, and Christ knew the minds of his disciples were very weak, so he endeavoured by every possible method to support them that they might not give way. His argument from the present day is the telling part: even now the remembrance of the cross is enough to make us tremble, were we not instantly met by the consolation that he triumphed in it, having obtained a victory over Satan, sin and death.

Henry notices the change of register the departure allows, that what follows was Christ’s table-talk with his disciples, who applied themselves to profitable discourse once the traitor had gone; and he draws from it the small practical lesson that we should make conversation with our friends at table serviceable to religion. Gill reads the same freedom in it, that Christ and his true disciples being now alone, he used a greater liberty of conversation with them. What the verse establishes before any of that begins is the paradox the whole Passion rests on: that to the eye of the world what follows is the disgraceful death of a condemned man, and in Christ’s own reckoning it is the hour of glory, his own and his Father’s.
32:
A change of tense carries the argument, and Ellicott builds on it. What is promised here belongs to the Father’s throne, and those words about glorifying him in himself point to God rather than to the Son of man. Ellicott’s formulation is careful: a humiliation by which God stands manifested to the world constitutes God’s honour in the person of the Son of man, and what succeeds it will be the Son of man’s honour in the person of God. Robertson concurs that God is both the fountain of such glory (John 17:5) and the one who bestows it after Calvary. Ellicott adds a textual note, that a majority of the best manuscripts omit this verse’s opening clause.

Barnes reads the sentence as a confident expectation rather than a condition. If the life and death of the Messiah be such as to manifest God’s perfections and show his goodness, truth and justice, then God will show that he approves the work; Jesus here anticipates that the Father will not suffer him to go without a proper attestation of his acceptance, and Barnes finds the attestation given in the miracles attending the death, the resurrection and the ascension.

On the last word of the verse Robertson says simply that there is no postponement now, first and quickly the cross and then the Ascension. Clarke looks for an earnest of it even within the Passion, finding one in the moment when the band that came to seize him fell to the ground at a word (John 18:6).

Calvin draws out the reciprocity the verse states. Christ concludes that he will obtain a triumph by his death, because his sole design in it is to glorify his Father; for the Father did not seek his own glory from the death of his Son in such a way as to leave the Son out of it. So Calvin promises what the sequel proved, that when the ignominy endured for a short time has been effaced, illustrious honour will be displayed in that very death, which is why the cross does not obscure Christ’s rank but chiefly displays it. For disciples about to see nothing but shame, the force of the sentence is in its last clause: the exaltation follows quickly, and they are to look through the one to the other.
33:
The address is what the expositors notice first. Robertson calls it an affectionate diminutive used by Jesus only here in this Gospel, though common in the First Epistle (1 John 2:1), as though the word had impressed itself on John and become his own. Clarke renders it beloved children, such as a fond mother uses to her most beloved babes, and adds the circumstance that made it possible, that now Judas was gone out he could use the epithet without any restriction of meaning. Barnes explains why the term fits here, as denoting both their need of teaching and guidance and the deep interest in their welfare that a parent feels. Lightfoot suggests Christ may have had Isaiah in mind, where the prophet says behold, I and the children whom the Lord hath given me, a saying he could use properly once the son of perdition had removed himself.

Augustine guards the saying against a misunderstanding the previous verse invites. Lest they should think God was going to glorify him in such a way that he would have no further converse with them on earth, he says that he is with them yet a little while: he would indeed be straightway glorified by his resurrection, but would not straightway ascend, and the Acts record that he was with them forty days afterwards. Origen reads the diminutive as a comment on their condition, that he calls them little children because their souls were yet in infancy.

On the harder clause, several note that Christ repeats to the disciples what he had already said to the hostile Jews (John 7:33; 8:21), and that the same words carry a wholly different intent here. Wesley supplies the qualification that makes the difference, that they cannot come not yet, being not yet ripe for it. Clarke takes the seeking of him as the distress they would feel for a few days in his absence.

Calvin reads the verse as warning and comfort held together. Since it was impossible that the disciples should not be deeply grieved at their Master’s departure, he gives them early warning that he will no longer be with them and exhorts them to patience; and to remove an unseasonable eagerness of desire, he declares that they cannot immediately follow. The tenderness of the name is doing work in that argument rather than decorating it, since by that gentle appellation he shows that his reason for departing is not that he cares little for their welfare. The same sentence announces the parting and cushions it.
34:
Augustine raises the obvious objection against himself. Had Moses not required as much already, writing that a man shall love his neighbour as himself? His reply looks to effect rather than content: Christ calls this new because he has divested us of an old humanity and clothed us with a new one, and because not every sort of affection renews whoever obeys it.

Robertson locates the newness elsewhere, in the practice and the measure. He sets the adjective against the old commandment of the First Epistle (1 John 2:7) and puts the distinction plainly: they had had it a long time, but the practice of it was new, and the new standard is the clause as I have loved you. Clarke presses that standard to its conclusion. Under Moses a man should love his neighbour as himself; Christ more than fulfilled the Mosaic precept, since he loved his neighbour not as himself but more than himself, for he laid down his life.

Barnes finds the newness in its function, the commandment being given as a badge of discipleship by which they should be distinguished from all others. Ellicott sets the contrast differently again, not against the Decalogue but against what Christ had just said to the unbelieving Jews: to them he had spoken of a place they could not come to, and to his own he gives the law of mutual love.

Calvin reads it as the exhortation that crowns the consolation, and makes it the proof the absence will demand: while he is absent from them in body, they are to testify by mutual love that he has not taught them in vain. Taken together the readings make the commandment old in substance and new in degree, in pattern and in office.
