The old law bade men love their neighbours as themselves; this bids the disciples love one another as Christ has loved them, with a love that stoops to wash feet and lays down its life. That is the standard the church is left with, and the one thing by which it was to be recognised.
35:
Barnes states the mark negatively before he states it positively, and the negatives are the point. The disciples shall not be known by peculiar rites or habits, nor by a form of dress or manner of speech, nor by austerities and unusual customs like the Pharisees or the Essenes, but by deep, genuine and tender affection. He adds that this is exactly how it fell out, since the thing eminently distinguished the first Christians and was remarked on by the surrounding pagans, who said: see how they love one another, and how ready they are to die for each other. Clarke cites Tertullian’s Apology for the very words, and makes the same contrast, that the followers of other teachers were known by their habits or some rite or point of austerity they had adopted, where Christ’s were known by this love.

Ellicott finds the choice remarkable in itself. The followers of great Teachers and Rabbis had their distinctive marks, and here is the distinctive Christian mark which all men should be able to read; and it is instructive that the characteristic sign of Christianity should be asserted by its Founder to consist not in any formulary or sign but in love. Robertson adds the test from Jerome, who reports that John in extreme old age repeated this command constantly and justified it by saying that it is the Lord’s commandment, and if it be fulfilled it is enough; Robertson draws the converse, that hatred of one another is an argument that we are not disciples.

Gill distinguishes three things the mark establishes, which are not the same. By it the disciples themselves know that they have passed from death to life; by it they know one another to be Christians; and by it all men, even the men of the world, will know whose they are.

Calvin makes the mark a test that can fail in two directions. Those who lay aside brotherly love and adopt new and invented modes of worship labour in vain, since Christ has laid down this and not that as the distinguishing sign. And Calvin explains why the subject needs so much space, that there is no greater agreement between love of ourselves and love of our neighbour than between fire and water; self-love is what has to be displaced before the mark can appear at all. The credential is therefore public and legible: where such love exists the world has its proof, and where it is wanting the profession is empty whatever else is sound.
36:
Gill notices what Peter does not respond to, and finds it telling rather than blameworthy. One might have expected him to take up what Christ had just said about love to one another; he passes it over entirely, not from inattention or dislike, since his whole conduct and his writings show how much he valued it, but because some words had dropped from Christ’s lips that left him uneasy, and he could think of nothing else until he had asked about them. Henry is less indulgent and turns it into a general fault, that it is common among us to be more inquisitive about things secret, which belong to God only, than about things revealed, which belong to us; more desirous to have our curiosity gratified than our consciences directed.

Chrysostom reads the question as love rather than curiosity. A great thing is love, he says, and stronger than fire; and the most fervent Peter, hearing that he cannot come, asks where his Master goes, not so much from a wish to learn as from a desire to follow. He observes that Christ answered not to the words but to the thoughts, which is how we know what the wish behind the question was. Augustine agrees that the disciple asks as one ready to follow, and notes that Christ saw his heart.

The reply divides a now from an afterwards, and Augustine makes the division the whole consolation. Christ does not say thou canst not, but thou canst not now: he intimated delay without depriving of hope, and indeed bestowed the hope he did not take away. His address to Peter is the memorable part: why dost thou hasten? The Rock has not yet established thee with his Spirit; be not lifted up with presumption, for thou canst not now, and be not cast down with despair, for thou shalt follow afterwards.

Clarke identifies both reasons for the delay, that Peter had not yet faith strong enough to die for him and that his work was not yet done, and he points forward to where the promise was kept (John 21:18). Ellicott puts the same thought in terms of order, that for Peter as for the others the place must be prepared and the way opened before they could follow. Calvin uses the exchange as a mirror: it shows how ignorant Peter was, who after so many warnings about Christ’s departure was as perplexed as if he had heard something new, and we are too like him, hearing daily all that is needful and then astonished when it comes to practice.
37:
Robertson marks the impatience in the adverb, since Peter asks why he cannot follow this very minute rather than at this time, a sharper word than the one Christ had used. Gill reads the question as dissatisfaction with the answer given, and Ellicott as entirely in character, Peter being impulsive and self-confident and impatient of the delay imposed on him, ready in the fulness of his love now, and not dreaming that in the moment of trial he will be found wanting.

Clarke supplies a guess at what Peter imagined was meant. He probably thought our Lord intended some long journey, with its inconveniences and fatigue, and felt quite disposed to follow him in it at all hazards; he saw no reason why he could not follow now, because he did not see our Lord’s meaning at all. Robertson adds that Peter, like the rest, had not yet grasped the idea of Christ’s death, and that, like Thomas, he was not afraid of danger; he had heard the words about the good shepherd laying down his life (John 10:11) and knew that such loyalty was the mark of a good disciple.

Calvin names the fault precisely and generalises it. By these words Peter declares himself dissatisfied with the answer; he is aware that he has been warned of his own weakness and concludes that his own fault is what hinders him, but he is not at all convinced of it, since men are naturally puffed up with confidence in their own value. The expression shows the opinion we entertain from our very birth, that we attribute more to our own strength than we ought; and the consequence Calvin draws is exact, that those who can do nothing venture to attempt everything without imploring the assistance of God.

Clarke puts the pathos of it in a sentence that anticipates the whole night: Peter was sincere but did not know his own strength, being willing at that moment to die and unable when the time came. His order of events is the theological point. Christ must first die for Peter before Peter can die for Christ; and no man should think he can do anything good without the immediate assistance of God.
38:
Gill reads the tone of the reply with some care, and rules out one possibility. Christ speaks these words as questioning not Peter’s sincerity but his strength, and not in derision but rather in pity, as though he had said: thou poor vain self-sufficient man, thou dost not know what thou talkest of. The question throws Peter’s own words back at him, and the gap it exposes is between the boast and the man rather than between the promise and the intention.

Lightfoot is precise about the prophecy, and corrects a reading that would make it fail. We must not understand it as though the cock should not crow at all before the denials, since the bird had in fact crowed twice before Peter had finished; the sense is that the cock shall not have finished his crowing. He explains the idiom from the Jewish doctors, who distinguished the cock-crowing into a first, a second and a third, a distinction not unknown among other nations either; and the period was not half over before Peter had denied his Master.

Calvin draws the lesson against presumption and is careful about its purpose. Peter’s confidence is rebuked not to crush him but to teach him, and through him the church, how feeble and frail the strength of men is when they lean upon themselves. The plainness of the prediction is itself a mercy, since when fulfilled it would both humble him and, by the fact of its fulfilment, confirm his faith in the Christ who had foretold it, which is the use Christ himself had already assigned to his predictions a few verses earlier (v.19).

So the supper that began with a basin and rose to a new commandment ends with the foretelling of a disciple’s fall, which is a sober enough close. But the warning is not the last word in the chapter. The earlier promise still stands that he shall follow afterwards (v.36), so that the denier will one day become the martyr; and the prophecy is given in advance precisely so that Peter, having fallen and wept, may remember the word and be restored rather than destroyed. The chapter that opened with love to the end closes with a love that will not let even the denier go.
